title: The Token slot conflates receipt tokens with converted assets, hiding whether an instance holds a claim or a different asset
content:
The `Instance Identifiers` schema pairs `Asset Supplied By Spark Liquidity Layer` with `Token`. In the lending instances the pair is a claim relationship: USDC to `aEthUSDC` (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.2.2.2.1.3/.4), USDS to `aEthUSDS` (.2.3.2.1.3/.4), USDC to `syrupUSDC` (.3.1.2.1.3/.4). The token is a receipt redeemable for the same underlying, and this is confirmed by the `Underlying Asset Address` matching the supplied asset.

The Ethena instance uses the same two fields to express something else: asset supplied USDC (.4.1.2.1.3), token USDe (.4.1.2.1.4). USDe is not a receipt for USDC; it is a separately collateralised synthetic dollar with its own peg and backing mechanism. Spark ends up holding a different asset, not a claim on the one it sent.

Because both cases occupy the same slots, the template cannot distinguish them. Two instances with identical field structure carry categorically different risks — counterparty and pool-liquidity risk in one case, issuer and peg risk in the other — and nothing in the identifiers marks the difference.

The tell is available but indirect: Ethena's `Underlying Asset Address` is deferred (.4.1.2.2.2) while its `Token Address` points at the USDe contract, and its outflow is rate limited where lending outflows are not. A reader has to reconstruct the economic type from those side-effects. Inventorying ecosystem exposure by reading `Asset Supplied` across instances would count Ethena as USDC exposure, which it is not once the mint completes.
description: For lending venues Token is a receipt on the supplied asset (USDC to aEthUSDC); for Ethena, supplying USDC yields USDe — the same field describes two economically different positions.
